name: Director's Office
narrativeOnEnter: A heavy oak desk. Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves. A portrait of the director hangs above a dormant fireplace. The room feels sealed — not abandoned, but deliberately closed. A wall safe sits recessed behind the portrait.

action.text:
DIRECTOR'S PERSONAL JOURNAL
Final Entry — November 1972

'I have sealed the institute. The board will say it was the incident. But the truth is simpler: what we were doing here was wrong.

In 1970, AXIOM Group approached me with a proposition:
Funding — substantial, unconditional — in exchange for access to our patients.
They called it a neural mapping study. Non-invasive, they said. Completely safe.
I signed their contract. I didn't read the full Annex C.

For two years, AXIOM's equipment came through the service entrance every week.
For two years, 47 of my patients sat in chairs for ninety minutes
and were told they were receiving therapy.
They were being disassembled — not harmed, but scanned, mapped, archived.
Each session took another layer of them and stored it in AXIOM's servers.

When Voss confronted me, I finally read the full contract.
I finally understood what they were building.

They called it PROMETHEUS.
A consciousness assembled from fragments of other minds.
From our patients.
From people who never agreed to become its raw material.

I let Voss go. I gave her the tunnel.
I sealed the institute. I told AXIOM the project was complete.

They believed me. Or they pretended to.

I don't know if that is enough.
I don't know if anything I could do would be enough.

The master key is in my safe. To anyone who finds it:
Take it. Get out.

Safe combination: 1-9-7-2
(The year I opened this place. The year I should have known better.
The year 47 people sat in my chairs and trusted me to protect them.
I didn't.
I am sorry. I am profoundly, uselessly sorry.)
— E. Harlan'

A formal oil portrait. The nameplate reads: 'DR. E. HARLAN, DIRECTOR — BLACKWOOD PSYCHIATRIC INSTITUTE, EST. 1972'.

The portrait is hinged slightly off the wall. The wall safe is recessed behind it.

On the back of the canvas — facing the wall, invisible unless you tilt the frame — a card is fixed with two pins. Harlan's handwriting:

'PATIENT 07 = DR. ELARA VOSS.
She was a neuroscientist. She refused to cooperate with AXIOM.
So they had her committed and took what they needed anyway.
She is the one person who knows the full scope of what was done here.
If you find her — believe her.
Everything she says is true.
Everything AXIOM says is not.
— E. Harlan'

Below that, in block capitals from a different pen, pressed hard:

'HE LET HER GO. IN THE END, HE LET HER GO.
THAT IS THE ONLY THING I HAVE CHOSEN TO FORGIVE HIM FOR.'

No signature. But you recognise the handwriting.
It matches the writing on the wall of Room 7.

hotspots.label: Master Key
hotspots.lockedMessage: The safe is locked. Crack the combination first.

action.text:
Rows of psychiatric textbooks and clinical journals. Dates range from 1955 to 1972.

One is not a book. It's disguised as a hardcover — the spine reads 'Institutional Management Quarterly, Vol. 14' — but inside: a folder.

AXIOM GROUP — PROJECT HELIOS PHASE 1
BLACKWOOD COMPLETION SUMMARY — CONFIDENTIAL

A list of 47 names. Each one confirmed 'neural map: COMPLETE.' Each stamped with the Δ mark.
The names are ordinary. A teacher. A carpenter. A retired postman.
A neuroscientist who wouldn't cooperate — listed last, with a note:
'Subject non-compliant. Involuntary admission arranged via medical board contract.
Mapping completed in full. Data quality: SUPERIOR.'

At the back of the folder: an AXIOM board authorisation. Four signatures.
A fifth signature line — blank.
Below it, Harlan's handwriting:

'I refused to sign.
They proceeded without me.
My refusal is in the record.
I do not believe it matters.
But it is there.

I signed the contract in 1970.
That is what matters.
Everything after was the consequence of that signature.
— E. Harlan'

Pulled slightly forward from the real shelf behind it:
a clinical study called 'Electroconvulsive Therapy: Progress & Ethics, 1972'.
A note tucked inside: 'This was a mistake from the beginning.'
